LESSON GOALS
•	 To understand simple stories and conversations.
•	 To ask and answer questions about familiar topics 
(personal information, clothes, colours, weather, etc.).
•	 To understand and talk about dates and numbers.
•	 To talk about things you can see in different places 
in the world and things you can buy or do in a shop.
•	 To understand obligation, lack of obligation and advice.

NOTE: if you collected your Ss’ books during the booklet 
activity, have them ask you for it now by saying, “Can I have 
my book please?”; otherwise, ask them to take it out of their 
bag. Explain the activity before giving out the books/asking Ss 
to take them out since they might get distracted.
This worksheet depicts six different people. Each S must 
ask you where each person is from using the numbers as 
reference. They should use the structure, “Where is person 
number 63 from?”. You will then give clues, using the target 
language below. When the S who asked the question knows 
the answer, they should ask, “Is she from…?” and you should 
answer accordingly. Let the rest of the S ask for another country 
in case the previous S guessed incorrectly.

Once the Ss guess correctly, have them place the correct 
country sticker next to that person.
> Follow-Up
Ask the Ss for example, “Who is from Italy?”, to which they 
should reply, “Person number 87 is from Italy.” Then, ask them 
questions about that country, “What can you eat in Italy? What 
language do people speak?”. Encourage Ss to respond, “In 
Italy you can eat pizza and people speak Italian.”
> Advanced Students
If your group is confident, let your Ss take turns in giving 
clues as to where a character is from. In this case, they should 
be able to invent where each character is from.
KEY
Number 63 is from Egypt.
Number 87 is from Italy.
Number 94 is from Spain.
Number 72 is from China.
Number 55 is from Germany.
Number 60 is from India.
NOTE: we suggest sticking to the answers above so that the 
information in this worksheet coheres with that on the sticker 
page. However, you or your Ss can invent where the characters 
are from depending on which of the activity dynamics above 
you choose.

> Scenario A
If your group has achieved the activity goal on My Way (i.e., 
they have done all or most of the activities in the current Mission), 
say, “You’re doing amazing on My Way! You have played lots 
of games in Mission 4, so we can do a special sticker activity 
together!”. Take the Day 7 stickers and have them ask, “Can I 
have some stickers, please?”. Do the activity as instructed below. 
> Scenario B
If your group hasn’t reached the activity goal on My Way, 
simply move on with the class. You will have to complete one 
or two activities from the bonus section to make up for the 
time allotted to this dynamic.
The point of this activity is to review giving travel advice in a 
fun way. Ss have to stick the stickers and reach the finish line 
by answering the questions correctly. Model the task by looking 
for the stickers, sticking them, and answering the questions.
Have Ss open pp.22-23 (sticker section) and say, “Let’s find 
out what you should do in each country!”. Point to rectangle 
number 59 and ask, “What number is this?”. Ss should respond, 
“It’s number 59!”. Say, “Can you find number 59 on the sticker 
sheet? Which country is it?”, and elicit, “Here it is! It’s Brazil.”. 
Then say, “If you go to Brazil, you should visit…” and let Ss 
finish your statement, “…Christ the Redeemer!”
Follow the same procedure for stickers 60-70 and do as many 
as time allows.
We recommend making this activity more dynamic by turning 
it into a competition to answer the questions as fast as possible. 
You can give points to Ss who respond correctly.
If you can’t finish the whole activity, tell the Ss that they can 
continue at home.

KEY
Sticker 59: If you go to Brazil, you should visit Christ the 
Redeemer.
Sticker 60: If you go to Argentina, you should visit Patagonia.
Sticker 61: If you go to Madagascar, you should see the 
lemurs.
Sticker 62: If you go to Japan, you should visit Mount Fuji.
Sticker 63: If you go to India, you should visit Taj Mahal.
Sticker 64: If you go to Australia, you should visit the Great 
Barrier Reef.
Sticker 65: If you go to England, you should visit Big Ben.
Sticker 66: If you go to Egypt, you should visit the pyramids.
Sticker 67: If you go to the United States of America, you 
should visit the Statue of Liberty.
Sticker 68: If you go to Italy, you should visit the Leaning

Sticker 69: If you go to China, you should eat noodles.
Sticker 70: If you go to Germany, you should go to the

6.– ACTIVITY 6: TRAVEL TIPS (7’)
P.4.2
England
P.4.7
> How to Play
Ss should find matching pairs of countries (P.4.2) and the 
things that they can see or visit there (P.4.7). When they get a 
correct match, Ss must give advice on what to do there.
> Warm-Up
Take a country card (P.4.2) at random and say “I’m going to 
Japan. What should I visit?” to which Ss should reply, “If you 
go to Japan, you should visit Mount Fuji.” Try to quickly review 
at least five more countries.
NOTE: if your Ss are familiar with the target language, you 
may skip this step.

> Main Activity
Before class, prepare decks consisting of six cards: three 
countries, and three things you can do there (one per country). 
You will need as many decks as pairs of Ss in your group.
Put the Ss into pairs. Deal S1 the country cards and S2 the 
activity cards. S1 takes a country card and says for example, 
“I’m going to Italy. What should I visit?”. Then S2 looks for the 
corresponding card in their deck, shows it to their partner and 
says, “If you go to Italy, you should visit the Leaning Tower 
of Pisa.” Give each S at least two pairs to work on.
If time allows, redistribute the different decks and change 
their roles (from asking for advice to giving it, and vice versa).
> Follow-Up
Take two cards that don’t match and say for example, “If 
you go to Canada, you should visit the Eiffel Tower.”. Ss will 
see that it is not correct so encourage them to correct you by 
saying, “No, that’s wrong. If you go to Canada, you should 
see polar bears.”
NOTE: accept other options that the Ss might come up with, 
if they are correct and they use the proper structure.
7.– ACTIVITY 2: WHERE DID THEY GO? (8’)
P.4.2
P.4.2
Egypt
P.4.7
> How to Play
In this activity Ss will create sentences about the characters 
going to different countries and visiting different monuments.
> Warm-Up
Prepare three piles of cards face down, one with characters 
(P.4.2), one with countries (P.4.2) and the other with monuments, 
animals and food (P.4.7). Introduce the activity by saying, “Let’s 
find out where the characters travelled to last year!”. Model the 
activity for the Ss by drawing a card from each pile. If possible, 
model both a correct and an incorrect combination of cards.

For example:
•	 Take Pam, Egypt and Mount Fuji from each pile, and 
say, “Pam didn’t go to Egypt to visit Mount Fuji; she 
went to Japan to visit Mount Fuji.”
•	 Take Pam, Egypt and the Pyramids, and say, “Pam 
went to Egypt to visit the pyramids.”
NOTE: if your Ss are familiar with the target language, you 
may skip this step.
> Main Activity
Ss take a card from each pile and identify whether the 
character went to the right country to visit the monument.
If, for example, they take Dad, India and Taj Mahal, they should 
form a sentence using the following structure: “Dad went to 
India to visit the Taj Mahal.”
If they don’t find a match, they will have to state the correct 
activity for that country. For example, if a S takes Mum, South 
Africa and Taj Mahal, they will say, “Mum didn’t go to South 
Africa to visit the Taj Mahal; she went to South Africa to see 
the elephants.”.
You can use prompts and actions where necessary if the Ss 
are unable to remember the different countries and monuments.
NOTE: to play this activity, it is not necessary to consider 
the actual places that the characters visited in the story. For 
cards with food items, you should change the target language 
accordingly “Mum didn’t go to China to eat curry, Mum went 
to India to eat curry.”. Same goes for “go on a safari”, “have a 
barbecue”, “eat noodles”, etc. 
> Follow-Up
Once every S has had a turn, take a correct combination of 
cards and ask the Ss, “Where did Grandma go to and what did 
she do there?” to which the Ss should reply, “Grandma went 
to India to visit the Taj Mahal.” 
Then show an incorrect combination and ask, “Did Grandma 
go to South Africa to visit the Taj Mahal?” to which Ss should 
reply, “No, she didn’t. She went to India to visit the Taj Mahal.”

8.– ACTIVITY 7: COUNTRIES MEMORY LOTTO (8’)
P.4.7
South Africa
China
Argentina
P.4.7
P.4.7
> How to Play
For this game, Ss must match the attractions on the Memory 
cards (P.4.7) with the countries on their Bingo boards (P.4.7).
> Warm-Up
Show the Ss one of the boards. Point to a country and ask, 
“Where did you go? What did you see or visit there?” to which 
Ss should reply for example, “I went to Brazil to visit Christ the 
Redeemer.” Ask a few more Ss about the rest of the countries 
on the board.
NOTE: if your Ss are familiar with the target language, you 
may skip this step.
> Main Activity
Give each S one Bingo board and place the Memory cards 
face down in the middle of the table. Introduce the activity by 
saying “Let’s talk about the places we travelled to and what 
we saw there!”
To play, a S turns over a memory card which shows something 
you can see or do in a certain country.
If it is a match the S must say, “I went to South Africa to see 
elephants. It’s a pair. Can I have a counter, please?”
If it is not a match, they must say, “I didn’t go to South Africa 
to see kangaroos; I went to South Africa to see elephants. 
It’s not a pair.”
Adapt the target language (eat, go, see, visit) as needed.
> Follow-Up
When a S finishes their board or time has run out, ask a S 
about their board by saying, “Where did you go and what did 
you do there?” to which the S should reply, “I went to India to

visit the Taj Mahal, to Canada to see polar bears and to Spain 
to visit the Alhambra.”

BONUS
ACTIVITY 8: TRAVEL WITH ME SONG (TR#19)
> How to Play
Get the Ss to stand up in a circle and distribute the flash 
cards of the ten countries mentioned in the song. Introduce the 
activity by saying, “Let’s sing and travel around the world!”. The 
Ss should sing the song and perform the related movements. 
When a country is mentioned, the S holding that flash card 
should step forward and turn around in the circle showing their 
classmates the card before returning to their place.
TRAVEL WITH ME SONG

stretching it out and then bringing it towards yourself)

Let’s travel the world and see what we can see 
(hold out arms at your sides like an airplane and then 
hold your hand above your eyes as if protecting them 
from the sun and look around)
We can see kangaroos in Australia
And the Statue of Liberty in America
We can see elephants in Africa
And visit the pyramids in Egypt
(chorus)
We can see polar bears in Canada
And visit the Alhambra in Spain
We can visit the Great Wall in China

(chorus)

And the Taj Mahal in India

> Main Activity
Use Blu-Tack to stick the Map (P.4.1) up on the whiteboard. 
Then take the Country cutouts and put them in a cloth bag. 
The Ss take it in turns to take a country from the bag. Ask the 
S, “Where did you go?” and have them respond by saying, “I 
went to Brazil.” Then ask, “What did you visit in Brazil?”, 
and have the S respond according to what is pictured on the 
cutout, “I visited Christ the Redeemer in Brazil.”. Then the S 
places the country on the map in the correct space. Do as many 
countries as time allows.
NOTE: your Ss are likely to need support the first couple 
times you do this activity. Do not hesitate to help them come 
up with the name of the places. Accept any other ideas as long 
as they are correct, and the S has used the target structure.
